domain: Energy Policy / Climate Mitigation / Technology Governance
topic_summary: Analysis of the contested role of nuclear power expansion in climate decarbonization strategy. The dispute centers on whether nuclear is a necessary complement to renewables for reliable baseload power, or a capital-intensive distraction that delays faster renewable deployment. The kernel is the legitimacy criterion for climate-mitigation technology selection.

key_entities: Nuclear power industry (existing fleet + new reactor designs)
Climate policy frameworks (Paris Agreement, net-zero commitments)
Energy grid operators (reliability and dispatch authorities)
key_tensions: Baseload reliability vs intermittency risk (nuclear advocates vs renewable advocates)
Capital allocation competition (nuclear construction vs renewable deployment)
Temporal urgency vs technology maturity (deploy-now renewables vs build-later nuclear)
key_mechanisms: Capacity factor differential (nuclear ~90% vs solar ~25%, wind ~35%)
Learning curve effects (renewable costs declining, nuclear costs stable/rising)
Grid integration requirements (dispatchable vs variable generation)
Regulatory approval pathways (nuclear licensing vs renewable permitting)
key_absences: Demand-side management and efficiency as alternative to supply expansion
Geopolitical constraints on uranium supply chains and enrichment capacity

fracture_scan.notes: F03 detected: grid_reliability_physics classified as mountain but storage technology advancement may reclassify to rope. Generated omega_storage_breakthrough to bound this uncertainty. Kernel structure validated: three readings hold genuinely distinct axioms about what grounds technology legitimacy (reliability vs velocity vs precaution).

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The shared commitment is that climate-mitigation technology selection must be grounded in a legitimacy criterion. All parties argue about WHICH criterion (reliability, deployment velocity, precautionary principle) should govern, not whether a criterion is needed.
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Interpretive legitimacy derives from different epistemic communities: grid engineers (reliability), climate scientists (velocity/urgency), environmental ethicists (precaution). No single authority adjudicates; policy outcomes reflect coalition strength.

readings.commitment: A technology is legitimate for climate mitigation if and only if it provides dispatchable, baseload-capable generation to ensure grid stability
readings.expected_structural_delta: Nuclear enters beneficiary set (high capacity factor); intermittent renewables require costly storage to qualify; victim set includes ratepayers bearing reliability costs

readings.commitment: A technology is legitimate for climate mitigation if and only if it can be deployed at scale within the remaining carbon budget timeline (2030/2050 targets)
readings.expected_structural_delta: Renewables enter beneficiary set (fast deployment); nuclear excluded or marginalized (construction time); victim set includes grid operators managing intermittency

readings.commitment: A technology is legitimate for climate mitigation if and only if its worst-case failure modes and legacy costs are bounded and reversible within a generation
readings.expected_structural_delta: Renewables enter beneficiary set (decommissioning is reversible); nuclear excluded (waste legacy, accident risk); victim set includes future generations bearing irreversible costs

axiom_contradictions.basis: No single framework can hold both 'grid stability is the binding constraint' and 'deployment speed is the binding constraint' as simultaneously true. One must be subordinated to the other in any coherent policy.

No single framework can hold both 'accept irreversible legacy costs for grid stability' and 'reject technologies with irreversible legacy costs' as simultaneously true. These axioms are mutually exclusive.

Velocity primacy accepts intermittency risk and storage uncertainty to maximize deployment speed; precautionary reading rejects technologies whose failure modes are not fully characterized. A coherent framework cannot hold both as binding constraints.
